questions.q: For a drug to be excreted it must be:
questions.exp: The page opens by stating that the drug excreted is ionised/water soluble/polar - the opposite of the requirements for absorption. (Book p15)

questions.q: The major organ of excretion is the ______, while the major organ involved in metabolism is the ______.
questions.exp: Kidneys are marked m/c organ for excretion and the note on the right says the liver is the m/c organ involved in metabolism. (Book p15)

questions.q: Of the drug excreted by the kidney, filtration accounts for _____ while tubular secretion accounts for _____.
questions.exp: The table headings give filtration 20% and tubular secretion 80% - secretion is the larger renal route. (Book p15)

questions.q: Unbound drug is excreted by:
opts: Filtration (+); it is not handled by tubular secretion (-)
Tubular secretion (+); it is not filtered (-)
Both filtration and tubular secretion equally
questions.exp: In the table's unbound drug row, filtration is marked + and tubular secretion marked -. (Book p15)

questions.q: Plasma protein bound drug is NOT filtered because of the:
opts: Negative charge of the basement membrane
Positive charge of the basement membrane
Large size of the drug molecule
Presence of P-glycoprotein in the glomerulus
questions.exp: Filtration is marked negative for plasma protein (negatively charged) bound drug, explained in the table as due to the -ve charge of the basement membrane which repels it. (Book p15)

questions.q: Plasma protein bound drug is excreted by:
opts: Tubular secretion (+), while filtration is negative (-)
Filtration (+), while tubular secretion is negative (-)
questions.exp: For plasma protein bound drug the table marks tubular secretion + and filtration -, so secretion is the route that clears protein-bound drug. (Book p15)

questions.q: Which statement summarising the renal excretion table is correct?
opts: Unbound drug is filtered; protein-bound drug is secreted
Unbound drug is secreted; protein-bound drug is filtered
Both unbound and protein-bound drug are filtered
Neither unbound nor protein-bound drug is secreted
questions.exp: The table splits the two: filtration handles unbound drug (+, secretion -), while protein-bound drug is handled by tubular secretion (+, filtration -). (Book p15)

questions.q: Apart from the kidneys and liver, some drugs are excreted through:
questions.exp: The page notes that some drugs are excreted through saliva and sweat. (Book p15)

questions.q: Filtration, being dependent on GFR, results in:
opts: A rate proportional to plasma concentration
questions.exp: The note states filtration is dependent on GFR and therefore gives a constant rate of excretion - the basis of zero-order elimination. (Book p15)

questions.q: The rate of drug elimination (RDE) is defined as the:
opts: Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body
Fraction of drug removed per half-life
Amount of plasma cleared of drug per hour
questions.exp: RDE = amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body - a rate, not a fraction. (Book p15)

questions.q: Rate of drug elimination is calculated as:
questions.exp: RDE = plasma concentration x clearance, so the rate of elimination rises with either higher plasma levels or higher clearance. (Book p15)

questions.q: In the units given for the RDE equation, plasma concentration is expressed as mg/ml and clearance as ml/hr, so RDE is expressed in:
questions.exp: The page spells out the units: RDE (mg/hr) = plasma concentration (mg/ml) x clearance (ml/hr). (Book p15)

questions.q: Plasma concentration, as described here, is:
opts: Concentration of drug present in each ml of plasma, i.e. mg/ml
Total amount of drug in the body in mg
Amount of plasma cleared per hour
Amount of drug eliminated per hour
questions.exp: Plasma conc = conc of drug present in each ml of plasma, i.e. mg/ml. (Book p15)

questions.q: Drug clearance is defined as the:
opts: Amount of plasma being cleared of the drug per hour
Amount of drug eliminated per hour
Volume of distribution divided by half-life
Concentration of drug in each ml of plasma
questions.exp: Drug clearance = amount of plasma being cleared of the drugs per hour, expressed in ml/hr. (Book p15)

questions.q: The two modes of drug dosing described are:
opts: Continuous IV infusion and intermittent dosing
questions.exp: Under drug dosing the page lists a. continuous IV infusion and b. intermittent dosing. (Book p15)

questions.q: On the concentration-time curve of a continuous IV infusion, phase I is:
opts: The slowly rising state (infusion), when absorption exceeds excretion
Steady state, when infusion rate equals elimination rate
The declining state, when excretion exceeds absorption
The phase of zero drug in plasma
questions.exp: Phase I is the slowly rising state of infusion; during it absorption exceeds excretion. (Book p16)

questions.q: On the infusion concentration-time curve, phase II is the steady state at which:
opts: Infusion rate equals the rate of drug elimination
questions.exp: Phase II is labelled steady state plasma concentration with 'infusion rate = rate of drug elimination'. (Book p16)

questions.q: Phase III of the concentration-time curve of an infusion is characterised by:
opts: A declining state (elimination) in which excretion exceeds absorption
A slowly rising state with absorption exceeding excretion
A steady state with equal infusion and elimination
questions.exp: Phase III is the declining state (elimination), during which excretion exceeds absorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: The infusion rate (dosing rate) is calculated as:
opts: Volume of distribution x Plasma concentration
questions.exp: Infusion rate = plasma concentration x clearance - simply the RDE equation applied at steady state. (Book p16)

questions.q: How many half-lives are required to attain the steady state plasma concentration during an infusion?
questions.exp: The page states that 4-5 T1/2 are required to attain steady state plasma concentration. (Book p16)

questions.q: According to the page, attainment of steady state depends on:
questions.exp: For continuous IV infusion the page states that steady state depends on volume of distribution. (Book p16)

questions.q: At steady state during a constant infusion, if clearance rises while the infusion rate is unchanged, the plasma concentration will:
opts: Fall, because infusion rate = PC x CL
Rise, because clearance adds drug to plasma
Remain identical because steady state is fixed
First rise and then stay constant
questions.exp: Rearranging infusion rate = PC x CL gives PC = infusion rate/CL, so for a fixed infusion rate a higher clearance yields a lower steady state concentration. (Book p16)

questions.q: Intermittent dosing is also known as:
questions.exp: Under intermittent dosing the page writes 'AKA maintenance dose'. (Book p16)

questions.q: The purpose of intermittent (maintenance) dosing is to:
opts: Give the dose after a certain period of time to maintain the plasma concentration in a steady state
Rapidly achieve the target plasma concentration at the outset
Avoid the need for any loading dose
Eliminate the influence of clearance on therapy
questions.exp: Dose is given after a certain period of time to maintain plasma concentration in steady state - that is the maintenance dose. (Book p16)

questions.q: The maintenance dose is calculated as:
opts: PC x CL x Time / f
PC x CL / f x Time
PC x f x Time / CL
CL x f x Time / PC
questions.exp: Maintenance dose = PC x CL x Time / f, with f the bioavailability. (Book p16)

questions.q: Unlike the loading dose, the maintenance dose depends on:
questions.exp: The page states intermittent (maintenance) dosing depends on clearance, whereas the loading dose was determined by volume of distribution. (Book p16)

questions.q: In the maintenance dose formula, f stands for bioavailability and its value for IV routes is:
questions.exp: The page notes f = bioavailability and f = 1 in IV routes, so no correction is needed for intravenous dosing. (Book p16)

questions.q: Half life (T1/2) is defined as the time taken by a drug to:
opts: Be completely eliminated from the body
Reach steady state during an infusion
questions.exp: T1/2 = time taken by a drug to decrease by 50% in plasma. (Book p16)

questions.q: Half life is calculated as:
questions.exp: T1/2 = 0.693 x vd/CL; equivalently T1/2 = 0.693/Kel. (Book p16)

questions.q: Half life is proportional to:
opts: Volume of distribution divided by clearance
Clearance divided by volume of distribution
Volume of distribution multiplied by clearance
questions.exp: T1/2 is proportional to vd/CL - a drug with a large vd or a low clearance has a long half-life. (Book p16)

questions.q: The elimination constant (Kel) is given by:
questions.exp: Elimination constant (Kel) = CL/vd - the reciprocal of the relationship used for T1/2. (Book p16)

questions.q: If the volume of distribution of a drug increases while clearance remains unchanged, the half-life will:
opts: Decrease, because more drug leaves the plasma
Remain unchanged, since T1/2 depends only on clearance
Become equal to the elimination constant
questions.exp: Since T1/2 = 0.693 x vd/CL, a larger volume of distribution with the same clearance lengthens the half-life. (Book p16)

questions.q: Zero order kinetics means elimination of:
opts: A constant amount of drug per hour
A constant proportion of drug per hour
An exponentially increasing amount per hour
An amount proportional to plasma concentration
questions.exp: Zero order kinetics = constant amount of drug eliminated per hour; first order = constant proportion of drug per hour. (Book p17)

questions.q: In the equation RDE = (PC)^n x CL, the value of n for zero order and first order kinetics respectively is:
questions.exp: The table gives n = 0 for zero order kinetics and n = 1 for first order kinetics. (Book p17)

questions.q: When the dose and clearance are constant, the rate of drug elimination is:
opts: Constant in zero order kinetics and proportional to plasma concentration in first order kinetics
Proportional to plasma concentration in zero order and constant in first order
Constant in both zero and first order kinetics
Proportional to plasma concentration in both orders of kinetics
questions.exp: With a constant dose the table gives RDE = constant for zero order, while in first order RDE is proportional to plasma concentration. (Book p17)

questions.q: If the dose is increased, the half-life in zero order kinetics and first order kinetics respectively:
opts: Increases in zero order; remains constant in first order
Remains constant in zero order; increases in first order
Increases in both zero and first order kinetics
Decreases in zero order; remains constant in first order
questions.exp: The 'if dose increases' row shows T1/2 rising (upward arrow) for zero order but remaining constant in first order; clearance stays constant in both. (Book p17)

questions.q: With increasing dose, the rise in plasma concentration is disproportionate with a risk of toxicity in zero order kinetics, whereas in first order kinetics the rise is:
questions.exp: In zero order, an increase in plasma concentration is disproportionate (risk of toxicity); in first order it is proportionate. (Book p17)

questions.q: Zero and first order kinetics are seen in drugs showing:
opts: Early saturation of elimination and late saturation of elimination respectively
Late saturation of elimination and early saturation of elimination respectively
No saturation of elimination at all
questions.exp: The table links zero order kinetics to early saturation of elimination and first order kinetics to late saturation of elimination. (Book p17)

questions.q: Zero order drugs at LOWER doses follow first order kinetics until saturation. This behaviour is therefore also called:
questions.exp: The exception row reads: at lower doses such drugs follow first order kinetics until saturation - hence aka pseudozero order. (Book p17)

questions.q: Drugs that follow first order kinetics at HIGHER doses:
opts: Become pseudozero order at low doses
Show a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration
Show a rising half-life with increasing dose
questions.exp: The table's exception row for first order kinetics states that at higher doses the drug follows zero order after saturation. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which of the following drugs are given as examples of zero order kinetics?
opts: Alcohol, theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin
questions.exp: The zero order example list is alcohol (true zero order), theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin. (Book p17)

questions.q: Most drugs follow which kinetics?
questions.exp: The examples column for first order kinetics says simply 'most drugs'. (Book p17)

questions.q: A patient on phenytoin has the dose increased slightly and develops toxicity with a very high plasma level. This is because phenytoin follows:
opts: Zero order kinetics, so elimination is already saturated and plasma concentration rises disproportionately
First order kinetics, so plasma concentration rises proportionately
First order kinetics with a shortened half-life
questions.exp: Phenytoin is listed among zero order drugs (early saturation of elimination), so a small dose increment produces a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration with risk of toxicity. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which drug is specifically labelled as 'true zero order' in the examples list?
questions.exp: The example list annotates alcohol as true zero order; phenytoin, theophylline, tolbutamide, heparin, methanol and warfarin are also in the zero order list. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which anticoagulants appear in the zero order kinetics list?
questions.exp: Both heparin and warfarin are listed among zero order drugs, unlike most drugs which follow first order kinetics. (Book p17)

units.title: The Rules of Excretion
units.guide: A drug can only leave the body when it is ionised, water soluble and polar - the mirror image of the rules for absorption. The kidney is the commonest organ of excretion and the liver the commonest organ of metabolism.

units.title: Filtration vs Tubular Secretion
units.guide: Renal excretion splits into filtration (20%) and tubular secretion (80%). Filtration only handles unbound drug and fails for protein-bound drug because the negatively charged basement membrane repels it - such drug is instead cleared by tubular secretion. Minor routes include saliva and sweat, and because filtration depends on GFR it proceeds at a constant rate.

units.title: Rate of Drug Elimination and Clearance
units.guide: RDE is the amount of drug eliminated per hour and equals plasma concentration x clearance, in units mg/hr = mg/ml x ml/hr. Plasma concentration is the drug per ml of plasma, while clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug each hour. Dosing is achieved either by continuous IV infusion or intermittent dosing.

units.title: The Three Phases of an Infusion Curve
units.guide: An infusion curve has three phases: phase I, the slowly rising state in which absorption exceeds excretion; phase II, the steady state in which infusion rate exactly equals the rate of drug elimination; and phase III, the declining state of elimination in which excretion exceeds absorption.

units.title: Infusion Rate, Steady State and 4-5 Half-Lives
units.guide: Infusion rate (the dosing rate) equals plasma concentration x clearance, which rearranges so that steady state concentration falls when clearance rises. Steady state takes 4-5 half-lives to be attained, and the book adds that it depends on the volume of distribution.

units.title: Maintenance Dose and Its Formula
units.guide: Intermittent dosing is the maintenance dose: it is repeated at fixed intervals to hold the plasma concentration in steady state and depends on clearance, being calculated as PC x CL x Time/f. Here f is bioavailability and equals 1 for intravenous routes.

units.title: Half Life and the Elimination Constant
units.guide: Half life is the time for plasma drug to fall by 50% and is calculated as 0.693 x vd/CL, so it is proportional to volume of distribution and inversely related to clearance - a bigger vd with the same clearance means a longer half-life. The elimination constant Kel is the reciprocal idea, CL/vd.

units.title: Zero vs First Order: Reading the Table
units.guide: Zero order elimination removes a constant amount per hour and first order a constant proportion per hour, expressed as n = 0 and n = 1 in RDE = (PC)^n x CL. Doubling the dose in zero order lengthens the half-life and raises plasma concentration disproportionately - hence toxicity - while first order kinetics stay proportionate. Zero order reflects early saturation of elimination and first order late saturation; zero order drugs behave as first order at low doses (pseudozero order), and first order drugs become zero order once saturated at high doses.

units.title: Zero-Order Drugs: Examples and Danger
units.guide: The zero order list is alcohol (true zero order), theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin, while most other drugs are first order. The danger is clinical: a small increment of phenytoin can push a saturated enzyme system and cause a disproportionate rise in plasma level with toxicity.
